title: In that sample, more exposure to a language went with an earlier spurt in it
summary: The same study found earlier single-language spurts when infants heard more of that language, and fewer spurts in a bilingual child's less-heard language.
body: In the Quebec study of 45 infants, more exposure to a language went with an earlier spurt in that language alone. Bilingual infants were less likely to show a spurt in their non-dominant language than in their dominant language. For vocabularies that combined both languages, monolingual infants and unbalanced bilinguals had earlier and steeper spurts than balanced bilinguals. The authors say this pattern fits accumulator accounts, which stress piling up experience, better than accounts that tie a spurt to a general cognitive change. That comparison is their reading of this sample. It is not a reason to rank a bilingual home as late.

sources.title: Testing Theories of the Vocabulary Spurt with Monolingual and Bilingual Infants
sources.author: Miranda Gomez Diaz, Laia Fibla, Rachel Ka-Ying Tsui, and Krista Byers-Heinlein
sources.note: Opened 2026-11-26. Supports the abstract on exposure, dominant versus non-dominant spurts, and the authors' statement that results better support accumulator models than cognitive theories.
